questions.question: Tell the story of the coelacanth and explain why it is called a living fossil.
questions.expected_answer: Scientists knew the coelacanth only from fossils and believed it had died out about 66 million years ago. In December 1938, a fishing boat caught one near East London. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer of the East London Museum saw that it was unusual, and Professor James Smith identified it as a coelacanth. It is called a living fossil because it looks very like its fossil relatives. More have since been found, including off Sodwana Bay.

questions.question: Describe two South African dinosaurs.
questions.expected_answer: Massospondylus was a plant-eater with a long neck, long tail and small head, up to about five metres long; its nests with eggs were found at Golden Gate. Heterodontosaurus was a small dinosaur, about the size of a turkey, with three kinds of teeth, including tusk-like fangs. Melanorosaurus was a bigger early plant-eating dinosaur.

questions.question: What is the Cradle of Humankind, and what has been found there?
questions.expected_answer: The Cradle of Humankind is a World Heritage Site in Gauteng, an area of limestone caves where many fossils of early human relatives and ancient animals have been found. Finds include Mrs Ples, a skull more than two million years old found at Sterkfontein in 1947, Little Foot, a very complete skeleton, and Homo naledi, from more than 1,500 bone pieces found in the Rising Star Cave.
